item.title: AI stocks drag markets down worldwide as oil prices climb to their highest since May
item.description: Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May because of worries about the war with Iran ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran. The S&P 500 tumbled 1.4 per cent following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Nasdaq composite was down 2.2 per cent, as of 10:45 a.m. Eastern time, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 0.6 per cent, or 295 points. AI-related stocks have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth. Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 9.7 per cent. It gave a range as its forecast for profit in the final three months of 2026 whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment. Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 6.4 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses. Tesla erased an early drop to rise 0.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 3.8 per cent. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 7.1 per cent, though it’s swung between gains and losses of roughly 4 per cent in each of the last two days. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6 per cent to US$111.60 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the US$97 to US$112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1 per cent It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. Worries about big debt affect almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors. But U.S. yields nevertheless sank Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.01 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could be a signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, though they got drowned out by the drops for the more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday. CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.8 per cent. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

item.title: Tesla drops as spending pullback clouds AI, robotics ambitions
item.description: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Tesla’s shares slid five per cent in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker’s reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk’s AI, robotics and autonomous-driving ambitions. The company on Wednesday lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about US$20 billion from more than $25 billion after spending far less than expected on AI and robotics in the third quarter, which led to a surprise positive free cash flow. The strong position may prove valuable as CEO Musk explores combining Tesla with the far more capital-intensive SpaceX. But “investors are likely to come away with mixed feelings,” J.P.Morgan analysts, led by Rajat Gupta, wrote in a note. “The delay helps near-term cash burn but also suggests delays in investments that matter for fruition of long-term opportunities.” Wednesday’s management commentary suggested spending will be ramped up in 2027 and 2028 as Tesla continues to fund robotaxi, Optimus, AI compute and Terafab milestones, the brokerage said. Tesla’s shares have declined about 14 per cent this year, in contrast to the Nasdaq’s roughly 15 per cent gain. The stock is about 23 per cent below its record intraday high of $498.83, reached in December 2025. Its valuation, however, remains well above peers: Tesla traded at 188.24 times its forward earnings estimates, compared with 6.58 for Ford and 5.16 for General Motors. “The risk is Tesla now enters a period of limbo while investors await news on a potential combination with SpaceX, which ... might face significant regulatory hurdles,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. (Reporting by Joel Jose in Bengaluru; Editing by Joyjeet Das)

item.title: Uranium sector offers compelling investment case: Brooke Thackray
item.description: Although the uranium sector has been moving lower in the stock market, the long-term contract price (term) of uranium has been moving higher. The red line in the graph below represents the long-term ...
item.content:encoded:
The uranium sector has a very strong fundamental profile to move higher over the long term, and demand is expected to continue to grow. Nuclear power is now considered a source of green energy and the world’s demand for energy is skyrocketing. The buildout of AI and the shift to electrically powered transportation have created new sources of demand for electricity.

“Electricity is at the heart of modern economies and electricity demand grows much faster than overall energy use in all scenarios. It rises by around 40 per cent to 2035 in both the CPS and the STEPS, and by more than 50 per cent in the NZE Scenario,” according to IEA World Energy Outlook 2025. Supply is not expected to be able to keep up with demand and is expected to decline. It takes 10 to 15 years to greenfield (develop from scratch) a uranium mine. Even if more uranium mines were started today, the output would not come online for many years to come. Most analysts and experts in the field acknowledge that there is going to be a substantial shortfall in uranium production. It is just a matter of how much of a shortfall and when it occurs. The graph below illustrates two different scenarios of world uranium production capability compared to nuclear reactor requirements. One is a low-production scenario (left) and the other a high-production scenario. In either case, there is a shortfall of uranium production. World uranium production capability Investing in the uranium sector in the stock market has been a frustrating experience. Although the price of uranium stocks has risen over the last few years, the uranium sector has moved lower since January 2026. This has happened as a number of positive announcements for the nuclear industry have been released in 2026. One of the reasons that the price of uranium has not risen rapidly, despite increasing demand and positive announcements, is that uranium mining companies have been reopening dormant mines. This option has been quickly dissipating as the nuclear mining industry has been increasingly using up its spare capacity. The uranium sector in the stock market has been moving lower since January of this year. Below is a graph of the performance of the Global X Uranium ETF (URA) that trades on the NYSE. It is a proxy for the uranium sector. The sector is down 16.8 per cent YTD and is down 42.5 per cent since its January high (as of end of day October 21). The sector has become dramatically oversold on a number of metrics. The uranium sector typically performs well on a seasonal basis in November through January. If the broad stock market manages to perform well in the near future, it would be reasonable to expect the uranium sector to also perform well and outperform the S&P 500. Global X Uranium ETF (URA) Although the uranium sector has been moving lower in the stock market, the long-term contract price (term) of uranium has been moving higher. The red line in the graph below represents the long-term contract price of uranium as posted by Cameco on its website. It is clear that the term contract price has been moving higher over the last few years, including 2026. The black line represents the spot price of uranium, which the market tends to focus on. The spot price has been more volatile than the long-term price. As shown in the graph, when the spot price is below the term price and the term price is rising, the spot price tends to play catch-up and also rises. If the term contract price continues its trend higher, it is reasonable to expect the spot price to also rise. A rising spot price will be supportive of the uranium sector in the stock market. Uranium price Investors find it hard to reconcile how the uranium sector could have such a positive profile with the falling price of the uranium sector in the stock market. Most investors have the uranium sector as a lower priority in their investment choices. The supply is known over the next few years as well as the demand, and as a result, investors have chosen to focus on other parts of the market, such as AI. The problem with ignoring the compelling case for the uranium sector is that when things change, the sector can move rapidly higher. It is difficult to predict when a catalyst may force a rapid revaluation for the uranium sector. In 2024 and 2025, the sector moved higher because of the overwhelming number of positive announcements that were favourable for uranium. Governments were announcing the creation of stockpiles and special programs to support the uranium industry. Hyperscalers were announcing deals to use nuclear power to power their AI data centres. Positive news releases for uranium are released almost daily. When the next slew of really big announcements will be released is not known. It can happen at any time. A constantly rising term contract price of uranium is supportive for the sector to move higher. The sector has become very oversold on a number of metrics and is poised to move higher. The case for investing in the uranium sector has become very compelling. item.title: CPP and OAS: Should you take the money or wait?: Stan Wong
item.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
item.content:encoded:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP). Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan. Do you actually need the income? Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn. The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes. Taxes can change the calculation Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback. For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320. CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting. Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient. The financial reward for waiting CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70. OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70. Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75. How long must you live to come out ahead? Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results. According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report , a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89. These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement. A total wealth planning decision There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense. Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives. The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security.
